opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because the power problem looks completely different depending on where the robot lives.

In a factory, you're in a controlled environment. You know where the charging stations are, and you know the shift patterns. You can design around a duty cycle: maybe the robot works a few hours, docks, swaps a battery or opportunity-charges during a lull, and goes back out. The floor is flat, the temperature is stable, and the tasks are repetitive, so you can model energy consumption pretty precisely. The engineering question there is really about uptime and cost per hour of useful work. Can I get a full shift out of it, or close enough that the economics beat a human or a fixed automation cell? Hot-swappable packs and good fleet scheduling solve a lot of that.

The battlefield flips almost every one of those assumptions. There's no guaranteed charging infrastructure, and the terrain is unpredictable. Climbing, carrying load, and moving over mud or rubble burn energy at rates that are much harder to forecast. Temperature extremes hurt battery performance. And energy isn't just an operational inconvenience there. It's a logistics and survivability issue. Every kilowatt-hour you need is something that has to be carried forward, protected, and resupplied, and the military already struggles with soldiers carrying too many batteries. So you have to think about things like hybrid power, foraging energy from vehicles or generators, very aggressive power management, and designing the system so it degrades gracefully rather than just stopping when it's low.

There's also a signature dimension. In a factory, nobody cares if your robot runs warm or hums. In a contested environment, heat and noise can make it a target, so the power system affects detectability, not just endurance.

So I'd frame it like this: in industry, power is an economics and scheduling problem. In defense, it's a logistics, resilience, and survivability problem. The underlying battery chemistry and actuators might be shared, but the system design and the trade-offs you're willing to make are very different. Honestly, energy density is still one of the biggest gating factors for humanoids being truly useful in the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is: the factory is a forgiving environment and the battlefield is not, and almost every design decision flows from that.

In a factory, power is basically a solved problem on the supply side. You've got grid power, you can run a tether, you can put charging stations every fifty feet if you want to. So the question isn't "how do we get energy," it's "how do we manage the duty cycle." A humanoid doing pick-and-place or tote handling might be drawing a few hundred watts on average, with spikes when it lifts or accelerates. The real constraints there are heat, battery degradation over thousands of cycles, and uptime. If a robot has to go sit on a charger for twenty minutes every two hours, your effective fleet size just dropped by maybe fifteen percent, and that's what the operations people care about. So you optimize for swappable packs, fast charge, predictable thermal behavior, and you accept a heavier robot because the floor is flat and nobody's shooting at it.

The battlefield flips all of that. There's no grid. Resupply is contested, it's dangerous, and it's slow. Every kilogram of battery you put on the robot is a kilogram a soldier or a vehicle had to carry forward, and every charging event is a logistics tail that someone can target. So you're optimizing for energy density and endurance first, and you're asking much harder questions about what the robot actually needs to do. Walking over rough terrain is enormously expensive compared to a factory floor. Carrying a load up a hill, dealing with mud, recovering from a stumble, those are all big transient draws. And then you have thermal and acoustic signature to think about, because a hot, loud robot is a visible robot.

And then there's the question of what happens at the edges. In a factory, a robot that runs low on power just stops and someone deals with it. In the field, a dead robot might be a robot you have to go retrieve under fire, or abandon with sensitive hardware on it. So you end up designing in things like graceful degradation, where the robot sheds capability instead of dying, or sleep modes where it can sit for days and wake up on demand. Those don't matter much in a warehouse.

The other thing I'd say is that people assume the battlefield version is just the factory version with armor bolted on, and that's exactly backwards. The factory robot can afford to be a generalist. The field robot almost has to be more specialized, because every watt spent on a capability you don't need in that mission is endurance you gave away. So you often see hybrid approaches: a legged platform that can ride on a vehicle, or that gets handed off between a wheeled base for transit and a humanoid form for the last hundred meters. That's really a power decision wearing a mobility costume.

astra-6.text:
I think the big difference is how much control you have over the environment. In a factory, you can plan around the battery. You can have charging stations, swap batteries, or schedule charging during downtime. The robot has a fairly predictable job, so you can work out how much energy it needs to get through a shift.

On the battlefield, you don’t have that predictability. You may need to move over rough terrain, carry a load, and operate for long periods without access to charging. And every extra battery you carry adds weight, which itself takes energy to move.

So I’d start with the mission: What does this robot need to do, for how long, and how are you going to resupply it? In a factory, power is largely an infrastructure and productivity problem. On the battlefield, it becomes a logistics problem that can determine whether the robot is useful at all.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big distinction is predictability. In a factory, you know the task, you know the environment, and you can plan around charging. You can have a robot work for a period of time, swap a battery, and get back to work. You can build the power infrastructure around it.

On the battlefield, you don’t necessarily have that luxury. The robot may need to travel over rough terrain, carry a load, and operate for long periods without a reliable place to recharge. And every battery you bring has to be transported by somebody.

So I’d start with the mission. How much work does the robot need to do, how far does it need to move, and how are you going to replenish its energy? Peak power matters, but endurance and the logistics behind it can be the harder problem.
